title: I Don't Want to Become Someone Who Feels Less
excerpt: A personal reflection on mental health, treatment, connection, and learning to build a life that feels like your own.
body:
"I don't want to be medicated for the rest of my life, but the bathroom floor was so cold."

I think one of the hardest parts of navigating mental health is learning to accept that sometimes you need help, even when you wish you didn't. There is a lot of conversation around mental health awareness, and rightfully so. We're encouraged to speak openly about our struggles, seek support, and remind people that they aren't alone. But I think we should also spend more time talking about what happens after someone recognizes that they're struggling. What does getting better actually look like? How do you build a life that feels fulfilling when your mental health requires so much of your attention?

For me, part of that answer has been learning to separate my mental health from my identity. I am more than my difficult days. I'm more than the moments when getting out of bed feels impossible, the days when my thoughts become overwhelming, or the times when I struggle to recognize myself. Those experiences are part of my life, but they are not the entirety of it. And I think remembering that distinction matters.

I don't want to be medicated for the rest of my life, but I also know what it feels like to reach a point where getting through an ordinary day becomes incredibly difficult. I remember the loneliness, the isolation, and the feeling that the world was continuing without me while I struggled to find the energy to participate in it. I'm not against medication. I believe in treatment, professional support, and having access to the resources that make living with mental illness more manageable. But I also think it's important to acknowledge that people can have complicated feelings about treatment. Wanting to understand your options, questioning your long-term needs, or worrying about your relationship with medication doesn't mean you don't appreciate the help you've received.

I don't want to lose the parts of myself that feel things too loudly. I want to learn how to manage those feelings without being consumed by them. And I think that's an important distinction when we talk about recovery. The goal shouldn't necessarily be to become someone who never experiences sadness, excitement, anxiety, disappointment, or overwhelming emotions. The goal is to develop the tools and support needed to experience those emotions without having them dictate the entirety of your life. I want to be able to have a difficult day without assuming my progress has disappeared. I want to recognize when I need support instead of waiting until I'm completely overwhelmed. I want to understand my own warning signs, communicate what I'm experiencing, and build routines that make it easier to take care of myself.

But I also want to enjoy my life.

I love seeing my friends. I love trying overpriced coffee shops and spending far too long trying to get the right picture. I love laughing until my sides hurt and realizing that I've been so caught up in conversation that I haven't checked my phone once. That seven-dollar cup of coffee carries a surprising amount of meaning for me. It's having somewhere to go, something to look forward to, and a reason to get dressed and leave the house. It's remembering that there is a world outside of my own thoughts, and that I am allowed to participate in it.

Sometimes, I think we overlook how important these ordinary experiences can be when discussing mental health. Having a support system matters. Having professional help matters. But so does having something to look forward to. So does maintaining friendships, finding hobbies, creating routines, and developing interests that have absolutely nothing to do with your diagnosis. I want to have a life that isn't organized entirely around how I'm feeling. I want to wake up excited about the day ahead. I want to make plans without constantly worrying that someone is upset with me. I want to enjoy a warm car after a long day, an unexpected text, or a conversation that makes me forget about everything else for a while. I want to experience happiness without immediately questioning how long it will last.

I also think we need to reconsider the way we understand strength when it comes to mental health. There is nothing particularly admirable about suffering in silence. There is no achievement in refusing help until things become unbearable. Sometimes strength looks like taking medication, attending therapy, asking someone to sit with you, or admitting that you're having a difficult time before it becomes a crisis. And sometimes strength looks like allowing yourself to enjoy a good day without feeling guilty about having one.

I've spent a lot of time thinking about love, too. About why we continue to care about people, why certain relationships change us, and why tenderness can remain even after someone is no longer part of our lives. I think that same capacity for love is important when we're talking about mental health. Connection can be an important part of feeling well. Having people who make you feel understood, relationships where you don't have to constantly question your place, and friendships that allow you to be yourself can make an enormous difference.

But I've also learned that I cannot rely entirely on other people to make me feel okay. I need to build a relationship with myself that doesn't depend on constant reassurance or the approval of everyone around me. I need to learn that someone being disappointed in me doesn't automatically mean I've done something wrong, and that a relationship changing doesn't mean I'm unworthy of being loved. I want to become someone who can experience disappointment without losing their sense of self.

I don't think the answer is to become less sensitive or to stop caring. I think it's learning how to care without abandoning yourself in the process. And perhaps that's where treatment, self-awareness, and personal growth meet. Not in the expectation that we'll eventually become immune to difficult experiences, but in developing the ability to move through them with more understanding, more support, and a little less fear.

I want good days to feel earned and not borrowed. I want bad days to pass without believing they mean something permanent about who I am. I want to understand that needing ongoing support doesn't mean I'm failing, and that managing a mental health condition doesn't mean I have to put the rest of my life on hold.

I don't know what the rest of my relationship with mental health will look like. I don't think anyone can promise that recovery will be straightforward or that difficult periods will never return. But I do know that I want to keep making plans. I want to keep seeing my friends, trying new places, taking pictures, falling in love with little things, and finding reasons to look forward to tomorrow. I want to build a life where taking care of my mental health is part of living, rather than the only thing I'm living for.

And maybe that's the point I've been trying to reach. I don't need to become someone who feels less. I need to learn how to live with what I feel, recognize when I need help, and give myself the same patience I would offer someone I love.

Because I know love exists. I know there is tenderness in me that has survived things I once thought would make me a harder person. I know there are people, places, and experiences that make life feel worth showing up for. I want to keep making room for all of them.

And I want to believe that the bathroom floor doesn't have to be where my story returns every time things get difficult.
